5: This module is the mechanical rulebook for WAKE✳︎.
6: 
7: The model is allowed to PROPOSE changes to durable state.
8: It is never allowed to decide whether those changes are valid.
9: 
10: That distinction is central to the experiment:
11: 
12:     model output = proposal
13:     governance = authority
14:     durable state = accepted history
15: 
16: The functions in this file are deliberately deterministic. Given the same
17: state and the same proposal, governance should reach the same decision
18: regardless of which model produced the proposal.
19: 
20: A model cannot persuade this module, reinterpret its instructions, waive a
21: requirement, or edit the rules during an invocation.
22: 
28: This gives WAKE✳︎ an important property:
29: 
30:     failure can become durable information
31:     without failure becoming durable state.
32: """

A key challenge is discovering sub-goals without relying on explicit intermediate rewards, enabling robots to decompose tasks and transfer skills across domains. We propose a dual mechanism for sub-goal discovery. The first is a top-down strategy that builds hierarchical sub-goal chains from general goals via intrinsic motivations. The second is a bottom-up approach that uncovers latent links between previously learned goals and perceptual classes. Implemented in the e-MDB cognitive architecture, our method was tested in both simulation and a real-world robotic manipulation task. Results show efficient sub-goal generation, transfer, and generalization.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.17979/spu.23.c53\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 5, 14]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.31234/osf.io/5dtx3\", \"title\": [\"Latent Learning Progress Drives Autonomous Goal Selection in Human Reinforcement Learning\"], \"abstract\": \"

Humans are autotelic agents who learn by setting and pursuing their own goals. However, the precise mechanisms guiding human goal selection remain unclear. Learning progress, typically measured as the observed change in performance, can provide a valuable signal for goal selection in both humans and artificial agents. We hypothesize that human choices of goals may also be driven by latent learning progress, which humans can estimate through knowledge of their actions and the environment – even without experiencing immediate changes in performance. To test this hypothesis, we designed a hierarchical reinforcement learning task in which human participants (N = 175) repeatedly chose their own goals and learned goal-conditioned policies. Our behavioral and computational modeling results confirm the influence of latent learning progress on goal selection and uncover inter-individual differences…

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=metrics+and+frameworks+for+evaluating+research+problem+significance+in+autonomous+AI+agents&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8_4\", \"title\": [\"Evaluating AI Agents\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8_4\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1\", \"title\": [\"A Brief History of AI for Scientific Discovery: Open Research, Metrics, and Autonomous Agents\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The history of artificial intelligence for scientific discovery is not a two year story about chatbots learning to write papers. It is a sixty year story about science repeatedly handing its bottlenecks to machines—first inference, then search, then measurement, then the full workflow—only to discover that each delegation solves one problem and exposes a harder one underneath. This paper traces that history from DENDRAL (1965) through the construction of open scholarly infrastructure (arXiv, Google Scholar, ORCID), the oracle breakthroughs of AlphaFold, and the current era of LLM driven autonomous research agents. Three interlocking threads are followed including AI as research instrument, AI for research infrastructure, and the reshaping of scholarly profiles and incentives by machine readable metrics. The central tension throughout is between automation and augmentation between building systems that replace human researchers and tools that amplify human creativity and judgement. The paper presents that the most consequential development is not any single tool but the emergence of an interconnected ecosystem where AI agents, preprint platforms, open source codebases, and citation infrastructure form a feedback loop that is fundamentally restructuring who can do science, how fast discoveries propagate, and what counts as a valid scientific contribution.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 3, 23]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8\", \"title\": [\"Reliable Evaluations for LLMs and AI Agents\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7508…
